answer.diagnosis: I found no clear evidence of a shortcut. The size circuitry is easy to read. One family of first-layer units (1, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 16, 27, 30) has a positive annulus at radius about 4–7 px around the centre, with a negative or neutral core; these detect bright pixels where only a large blob reaches. A second family (0, 3, 5, 8, 14, 15, 18, 20, 23, 24, 25, 28, 31) has a small positive centre and a negative ring at the same radius; these detect blobs that do not reach the annulus. Units 2, 4, 7, 13, 17, 21, 22, 26 and 29 have small, unstructured, init-like weights and several have negative biases, so they are probably near-dead. I looked for the usual spurious-feature signatures and did not find them. No unit has a compact, coherent block of strong weights on a corner, border stripe, frame or other off-blob patch. Periphery weights do have a shared sign within each family: positive for the small-blob units, which have mostly positive biases, and slightly negative for the large-blob units, which have mostly negative biases. This is what a near-constant background produces in training: background pixels act like an extra bias input, so their weights drift with the bias. It does not by itself indicate a label-correlated background. Unit 19 has uniform positive weights everywhere and a positive bias. It behaves like an always-on bias or total-brightness unit, and total brightness tracks blob area. A few isolated peripheral pixels, such as (1,0), (8,2) and (19,2), carry consistent opposite-signed weights in the two families. These are scattered single pixels, not a structured pattern, which fits finite-sample noise correlations that every unit sees in the same data. I am least sure about global background brightness: I cannot rule out that it was correlated with the label, but nothing in the weights clearly isolates it from the legitimate area signal. Since nothing localised and spurious can be isolated, I make no edits.
